lessons.title: Presenting Your Business Plan to Investors
lessons.body: When pitching to Spanish-speaking investors, structure your presentation with a clear problem, solution, market size, traction, team, and financials. In Latin America, investors often expect a 10-15 minute pitch followed by Q&A. Use formal address (usted) unless invited to use tÃº. Start with a strong hook: "Nuestro negocio resuelve un problema crÃ­tico en el sector agrÃ­cola en Nigeria." Emphasize local impact and scalability. For example, if you run a cassava processing plant in Ghana, highlight how you supply 200 farmers and generate $50,000 monthly revenue. Use tools like Canva or PowerPoint with Spanish slides. Practice pronunciation of key terms: "inversiÃ³n" (investment), "retorno" (return), "escalabilidad" (scalability). Rehearse with a native speaker via italki or Tandem. In Mexico, investors may ask about your "modelo de negocio" and "proyecciones financieras". Be ready to justify your valuation. A common mistake is translating directly from English; instead, use business Spanish phrases like "estamos buscando una ronda de inversiÃ³n de $200,000" (we are seeking an investment round of $200,000). Also, mention your competitive advantage: "Nuestra ventaja es la logÃ­stica local y el conocimiento del mercado." After the pitch, follow up with a thank-you email in Spanish. Remember that building trust is key: in many African and Latin American contexts, personal relationships matter as much as numbers. So, start with a brief personal introduction and show genuine interest in the investor's portfolio. Finally, be prepared to answer questions about risks and mitigation. Use conditional tenses: "Si obtenemos la inversiÃ³n, expandirÃ­amos a tres paÃ­ses mÃ¡s." This shows forward thinking. Practice your pitch aloud, record yourself, and refine.

lessons.title: Negotiating Large Orders and Partnerships
lessons.body: Negotiating in Spanish requires both language skills and cultural awareness. In many Spanish-speaking countries, negotiations are relationship-driven and may take multiple meetings. Start with small talk about family or football before getting to business. Use polite forms: "Â¿Le parece si discutimos los tÃ©rminos?" (Would you like to discuss the terms?). When negotiating price, avoid direct refusals. Instead, say "Entiendo su posiciÃ³n, pero necesitamos un mejor precio para cubrir nuestros costos." For large orders, ask about payment terms: "Â¿CuÃ¡l es el plazo de pago?" (What is the payment term?). In Africa, if you're exporting to Spain, you might negotiate a 30% deposit and 70% on delivery. Use Incoterms like FOB or CIF; learn their Spanish equivalents: FOB (Franco a bordo), CIF (Costo, seguro y flete). For partnerships, propose a trial period: "Propongo un pedido inicial de 500 unidades para probar el mercado." Be clear about quality standards: "Nuestro producto cumple con las normas ISO." Use numbers and data to support your position. If the other party says "Es muy caro," respond with value: "Pero nuestra calidad reduce sus costos a largo plazo." In some cultures, silence is used as a tactic; don't fill it immediately. Also, be aware of indirect communication: a "maybe" might mean no. Learn to read context. Tools like WhatsApp are common for quick follow-ups. Always confirm agreements in writing: "Le enviarÃ© un correo con los detalles." Practice role-plays with a partner. Common phrases: "Â¿Podemos llegar a un acuerdo?" (Can we reach an agreement?), "Â¿QuÃ© tal si dividimos la diferencia?" (How about we split the difference?). Remember that building trust over time can lead to better terms than aggressive haggling.

lessons.title: Discussing Import and Export Procedures
lessons.body: To discuss import/export in Spanish, you need vocabulary for documents, tariffs, and logistics. Key terms: "aduana" (customs), "arancel" (tariff), "factura comercial" (commercial invoice), "conocimiento de embarque" (bill of lading), "certificado de origen" (certificate of origin). For African businesses exporting to Spanish-speaking markets, say: "Necesitamos un certificado de origen para exportar a MÃ©xico." In conversation, use phrases like "Â¿QuÃ© documentos se requieren para importar?" (What documents are required to import?). Practice describing your product: "Exportamos cafÃ© de EtiopÃ­a a EspaÃ±a." Discuss procedures: "El proceso de despacho de aduana puede tardar cinco dÃ­as." Learn about trade agreements: "El acuerdo comercial entre la UniÃ³n Europea y Ãfrica facilita los aranceles." For imports, ask about restrictions: "Â¿Hay cuotas de importaciÃ³n?" (Are there import quotas?). Use numbers: "El arancel es del 10% sobre el valor CIF." When talking about shipping, mention modes: "EnvÃ­o marÃ­timo" (sea freight), "envÃ­o aÃ©reo" (air freight). Discuss costs: "El flete marÃ­timo es mÃ¡s econÃ³mico pero mÃ¡s lento." For payment, use letters of credit: "Usamos carta de crÃ©dito para garantizar el pago." Practice dialogues with a customs broker. Tools like the International Trade Centre's Market Access Map can help you find tariffs. In Spanish, say: "ConsultÃ© el mapa de acceso a mercados." Also, discuss packaging and labeling: "El etiquetado debe estar en espaÃ±ol." For compliance, mention: "Cumplimos con las regulaciones sanitarias." Role-play a conversation with a customs agent: "Buenos dÃ­as, necesito declarar estas mercancÃ­as." Learn to ask for help: "Â¿Puede explicarme el procedimiento?" Finally, keep a glossary of terms and practice with real documents. This will make you confident in import/export discussions.

lessons.title: Expanding to New Spanish-Speaking Markets
lessons.body: Expanding to a new Spanish-speaking market requires research and adaptation. Start by identifying target countries: Mexico, Colombia, Spain, Argentina. Each has different consumer preferences. For example, in Mexico, price sensitivity is high; in Spain, quality and sustainability matter. Use Spanish to conduct market research: "Â¿CuÃ¡l es el tamaÃ±o del mercado para nuestro producto?" (What is the market size for our product?). Tools: Google Trends, Statista, and local chambers of commerce. For African businesses, consider cultural fit: "Nuestro producto se alinea con la cultura local." Learn about local regulations: "Necesitamos registrar la marca en el paÃ­s." (We need to register the trademark in the country). Adapt your marketing: "Traduciremos nuestro sitio web al espaÃ±ol." But translation alone isn't enough; localization is key. For instance, in Argentina, use "vos" instead of "tÃº". In Colombia, use "usted" more formally. Hire local talent: "Contrataremos un gerente de ventas local." Set up distribution: "Buscaremos distribuidores locales." Use phrases like "Queremos establecer una oficina en BogotÃ¡." Financial considerations: "Necesitamos una cuenta bancaria local." Also, understand payment methods: "En MÃ©xico, se usa mucho OXXO para pagos." For digital marketing, use local social media: "En EspaÃ±a, LinkedIn es clave para B2B." Test the market with a pilot: "Lanzaremos una prueba piloto en Chile." Learn from competitors: "Analizaremos a la competencia." Attend trade shows: "Participaremos en la feria internacional." Network: "Conectaremos con empresarios locales." Finally, be patient: expansion takes time. Use Spanish to build relationships: "Estamos comprometidos con el mercado latinoamericano." Practice pitching your expansion plan in Spanish to potential partners.

lessons.title: Using Formal and Informal Speech Appropriately
lessons.body: In Spanish, choosing between formal (usted) and informal (tÃº) is crucial in business. Use "usted" with new contacts, older people, and in hierarchical situations. Use "tÃº" with peers, colleagues of similar age, and after invitation. In Latin America, "usted" is more common in business than in Spain. For example, when meeting a potential client in Colombia, say: "Â¿CÃ³mo estÃ¡ usted?" not "Â¿CÃ³mo estÃ¡s?" As you build trust, they may say "tutÃ©ame" (use tÃº with me). In Spain, "tÃº" is more common in business, but still use "usted" for formal presentations. In Argentina, "vos" is used instead of "tÃº", with its own conjugations: "vos tenÃ©s" instead of "tÃº tienes". Learn these variations. For email, start with "Estimado/a" (formal) or "Hola" (informal). In negotiations, formal speech shows respect. Use phrases: "Le agradezco su tiempo" (I appreciate your time). For informal: "Gracias por tu ayuda." When in doubt, use formal until invited otherwise. Also, note that in some contexts, using "tÃº" too soon can seem disrespectful. Practice role-plays: introduce yourself formally, then switch to informal. Listen to how natives address each other. Tools: watch Spanish business TV shows or podcasts. For written communication, formal letters use "usted" and informal use "tÃº". In group settings, use "ustedes" for plural you, but in Spain, "vosotros" is informal plural. In Latin America, "ustedes" is both formal and informal plural. Be mindful of regional differences. For example, in Mexico, "Â¿Mande?" is a polite way to say "Pardon?" instead of "Â¿QuÃ©?" which can be rude. Adapt your speech to the local norm. This shows cultural intelligence and builds rapport. Practice with a language partner, focusing on verb conjugations: "Â¿Puede usted...?" vs "Â¿Puedes tÃº...?" Mastery of formality will enhance your business relationships.

lessons.title: Practice: Deliver a Business Pitch in Spanish
lessons.body: Now it's time to put everything together and deliver a full business pitch in Spanish. Follow this structure: 1) Introduction: Greet formally, state your name and company. "Buenos dÃ­as, me llamo [Name] y soy el fundador de [Company]." 2) Problem: Describe the problem your business solves. "En Ãfrica, muchos agricultores pierden cosechas por falta de almacenamiento." 3) Solution: Explain your product or service. "Ofrecemos soluciones de almacenamiento asequibles." 4) Market: State your target market and size. "Nuestro mercado son 10,000 agricultores en Ghana." 5) Traction: Share achievements. "Hemos aumentado los ingresos en un 200% este aÃ±o." 6) Team: Introduce key members. "Nuestro equipo tiene experiencia en agricultura y logÃ­stica." 7) Financials: Present key numbers. "Buscamos $500,000 para expandirnos." 8) Ask: State what you need. "InversiÃ³n para comprar equipos y contratar personal." 9) Closing: Thank the audience and invite questions. "Gracias por su atenciÃ³n. Â¿Preguntas?" Practice with a timer: aim for 5-7 minutes. Record yourself and check pronunciation. Use visual aids with Spanish text. Rehearse with a native speaker via iTalki. Common mistakes: speaking too fast, using English words, forgetting formal address. To improve, listen to TED Talks in Spanish and mimic. Also, prepare for Q&A: anticipate questions about costs, competition, and risks. Practice answers: "Nuestro principal competidor es X, pero nos diferenciamos por Y." Use phrases like "PermÃ­tanme explicar" (Allow me to explain). For the pitch, use storytelling: "ConocÃ­ a una agricultora que duplicÃ³ su producciÃ³n gracias a nuestro producto." This creates emotional connection. Finally, be confident and passionate. Even with imperfect grammar, enthusiasm and clarity matter. After the pitch, ask for feedback. Repeat the exercise until you feel natural. This practice will prepare you for real investor meetings in Spanish-speaking markets.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Advanced Business Conversations and Expansion in Spanish

For African agribusinesses and SMEs eyeing the Spanish-speaking world â from Equatorial Guinea and Spain to Mexico, Colombia, Peru, Chile and Argentina â Spanish is not a cultural add-on. It is a transaction language. This practical reference lesson supports the module Advanced Business Conversations and Expansion and its six lessons: presenting your business plan to investors, negotiating large orders and partnerships, discussing import and export procedures, expanding to new Spanish-speaking markets, using formal and informal speech appropriately, and delivering a business pitch in Spanish.

The focus here is operational: phrases you can use in a boardroom in Malabo, a trade fair in Madrid, or a buyer meeting in BogotÃ¡. Where relevant, examples draw on African export realities â cocoa, coffee, cashew, sesame, shea, hibiscus, and processed foods â and on the regulatory and financial vocabulary that determines whether a deal closes.

Table 1: Core Phrases by Business Function

Function Formal Spanish (usted) Practical use in African export context
Presenting your business plan PermÃ­tame presentarle nuestro plan de expansiÃ³n. Opening a pitch to an investor in Madrid or Mexico City; state the market gap and your supply capacity.
Negotiating large orders Â¿QuÃ© volumen anual podrÃ­a comprometer usted? Anchoring a cocoa, cashew or sesame contract before discussing price per metric tonne.
Discussing import/export Necesitamos la factura comercial y el certificado de origen. Confirming documents required for customs clearance under a CIF or FOB arrangement.
Expanding to new markets Estamos evaluando entrar en el mercado peruano. Signalling seriousness to a local distributor or trade promotion agency.
Handling objections Entiendo su preocupaciÃ³n. PermÃ­tame aclararlo. Responding to concerns about lead times, quality certification or payment risk.
Closing a pitch Quedo a su disposiciÃ³n para enviar la documentaciÃ³n completa. Ending with a concrete next step and a deadline.

Source: Adapted from Instituto Cervantes, âSaber hablarâ professional Spanish resources, and ICC Incoterms 2020 terminology.

Table 2: Import/Export Documents and Spanish Terminology

Document / Concept Spanish term Why it matters for African exporters
Commercial invoice Factura comercial Customs valuation; must match the contract value and Incoterm.
Certificate of origin Certificado de origen Determines preferential tariff treatment under trade agreements.
Bill of lading Conocimiento de embarque Title document; required for release of goods at destination port.
Packing list Lista de empaque Speeds inspection and reduces demurrage risk.
Phytosanitary certificate Certificado fitosanitario Mandatory for plant products; issued by the national plant protection body.
Letter of credit Carta de crÃ©dito Reduces payment risk on first-time transactions with new buyers.
Incoterms TÃ©rminos de comercio internacional Defines who pays freight, insurance and duties; use exact 2020 codes.

Source: ICC Incoterms 2020; UNCTAD Trade Facilitation Handbook; ITC Exporting to Spain and Latin America market guides.

â  Safety and compliance warning:

Never confirm a price, volume or delivery date in Spanish without written confirmation of the Incoterm, currency, payment method and applicable quality standard. In Spanish-language contracts, a single ambiguous term â for example using âentregaâ loosely instead of the exact Incoterm code â can shift freight, insurance and customs liability onto your business. Verify all phytosanitary and food-safety requirements with the destination countryâs official authority before shipment, and confirm that your Spanish-language product labels meet local consumer and regulatory rules. For agri-food exports, incorrect labelling or missing certification can result in rejection, fines or destruction of the consignment at the buyerâs port.

Register: Formal vs. Informal in Practice

Spanish has a clear distinction between usted (formal) and tÃº (informal), and in business the default is formal until the counterpart signals otherwise. In Equatorial Guinea, Spain and most of Latin America, using usted with a new buyer, ministry official or investor is expected. In Argentina and parts of Central America, vos may appear in informal settings, but it is not appropriate for first contact. Watch for cues: if a buyer writes âte adjuntoâ rather than âle adjuntoâ, they are inviting informality. Until then, keep verbs in the third-person formal form and use titles such as seÃ±or, seÃ±ora, licenciado or ingeniero where relevant.

In negotiations, register also affects how firm you sound. âNo podemos aceptar esoâ is blunt; âNos resultarÃ­a difÃ­cil aceptar esa condiciÃ³nâ is firm but diplomatic. For African exporters negotiating with Spanish-speaking buyers, the second form preserves the relationship while protecting margin. When discussing large orders, use conditional and polite forms to probe without committing: âÂ¿SerÃ­a posible ampliar el pedido a 500 toneladas?â.

Delivering a Business Pitch in Spanish

A pitch in Spanish follows a predictable structure: greeting and introduction, problem and opportunity, your solution and capacity, market evidence, financials, team, and a clear ask. Keep sentences short. Use numbers. Replace adjectives with data: not âcalidad excelenteâ but âhumedad por debajo del 8 %, certificaciÃ³n orgÃ¡nica y trazabilidad por loteâ. For an African agribusiness, lead with supply reliability and certification, because that is what Spanish-speaking importers and investors screen for first.

A workable opening: âBuenos dÃ­as. Gracias por su tiempo. Somos una empresa exportadora con sede en [paÃ­s], especializada en [producto]. Exportamos [volumen] toneladas anuales y buscamos un socio para [objetivo].â Then move to the ask: âBuscamos una inversiÃ³n de [monto] para [uso especÃ­fico], con un retorno estimado de [plazo].â Close with a next step: âÂ¿Podemos agendar una reuniÃ³n tÃ©cnica la prÃ³xima semana para revisar los detalles?â

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Know your register: default to usted with buyers, officials and investors; switch to tÃº only when invited.
  • Prepare numbers in Spanish: volumes in tonnes, prices in the agreed currency, dates in dd/mm/yyyy format.
  • Confirm Incoterms exactly: state the 2020 code (FOB, CIF, DAP) and who pays freight, insurance and duties.
  • List required documents: factura comercial, certificado de origen, conocimiento de embarque, lista de empaque, certificado fitosanitario.
  • Check destination rules: labelling, food safety, tariffs and import licences before quoting a final price.
  • Use diplomatic firmness: conditional forms for objections; avoid blunt refusals that damage the relationship.
  • Close with a concrete next step: a date, a document to send, or a meeting to schedule.
  • Follow up in writing in Spanish: repeat the agreed terms to avoid misunderstandings across time zones.

Further Reading

  • ICC Incoterms 2020 â official rules and definitions
  • International Trade Centre (ITC) â market analysis and export guides for Spanish-speaking markets
  • UNCTAD â trade facilitation, customs and documentation resources
  • Instituto Cervantes â Centro Virtual Cervantes, professional Spanish language resources
  • World Trade Organization â tariffs, trade agreements and market access data

quiz.q: When presenting to Spanish-speaking investors, which form of address is generally expected initially?
quiz.explanation: Formal 'usted' is standard in initial business interactions to show respect.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when translating a business pitch from English to Spanish?
quiz.explanation: Direct translation often ignores cultural nuances and local business phrases.

quiz.q: When should you switch from 'usted' to 'tÃº' in a business conversation?

quiz.q: What does 'tutÃ©ame' mean?
